blocks.title: Vernalisation
blocks.text: Biennial and perennial plants are stimulated to flower by exposure to low temperature; this is vernalisation. The low-temperature stimulus is received by the shoot apex of a mature stem or by the embryo of the seed, not by the leaves as in photoperiodism.

For some plants vernalisation is an absolute requirement; in others it simply assists in inducing flowering. The duration of the low-temperature (chilling) treatment varies from four days to three months, and a temperature of about 4 degrees Celsius is very effective. It stimulates the production of a hormone, vernalin, which induces vernalisation.

Photoperiodism and vernalisation synchronise the reproductive behaviour of plants with their environment, ensuring reproduction at favourable times of year. They also ensure that the members of a species flower at the same time, encouraging cross-pollination and so genetic variability.

blocks.caption: Vernalisation against photoperiodism
rows: Low temperature, about 4 degrees Celsius for four days to three months
Shoot apex of a mature stem, or the embryo of the seed
Florigen, carried in the phloem to the buds

blocks.prompt: Winter wheat sown in spring grows but does not flower, while the same wheat sown in autumn flowers the next summer. Explain.
blocks.explanation: Winter wheat needs vernalisation: its shoot apex or embryo must receive a period of cold, near 4 degrees Celsius, to produce vernalin and become able to flower. Autumn sowing gives it the winter chill; spring sowing does not, so it stays vegetative.

items: Vernalisation is the induction of flowering in biennials and perennials by cold (about 4 degrees Celsius, four days to three months), received by the shoot apex or seed embryo, through the hormone vernalin; it is essential in some plants and helpful in others.
With photoperiodism it times reproduction to favourable seasons and synchronises flowering within a species for cross-pollination and genetic variability.
